Financial clarity, control and planning can help break the cycle.

posts.text:
WHEN SURVIVAL BECOMES THE BUSINESS STRATEGY

When business owners spend more time deciding which bills to pay than planning how to grow, something fundamental has changed.

For many UK businesses, the economic environment is becoming increasingly challenging. Entrepreneurs who once focused on expansion, innovation and creating employment are now concentrating on meeting their immediate financial obligations.

The pressure is coming from multiple directions:

• Rising employment costs, including employer's National Insurance contributions.
• VAT, PAYE and Corporation Tax obligations.
• Increasing energy, rent and supplier costs.
• Business rates and other operating expenses.
• Delayed customer payments.
• The cost of borrowing and limited access to affordable finance.

These pressures rarely occur in isolation.

The domino effect across the UK economy

When one company delays payment, its suppliers may struggle to meet their own commitments. This creates a chain reaction throughout the supply network, affecting businesses that might otherwise be commercially viable.

Investment is postponed. Recruitment is reconsidered. Expansion plans are put on hold.

Business owners increasingly find themselves managing financial pressure rather than developing their businesses.

How can businesses regain financial stability?

Businesses cannot control government taxation policy, energy markets or the wider economy. However, they can improve their financial visibility, strengthen internal controls, negotiate commercial terms, manage working capital more effectively and make better-informed strategic decisions.

This requires more than historical financial reporting.

It requires forward-looking financial management, realistic forecasting, scenario analysis and a clear understanding of the financial consequences of every major business decision.

At AU Finance & Advisory, we believe the role of a finance professional extends beyond bookkeeping, statutory accounts and tax compliance.

Our purpose is to help business owners understand their financial position, identify practical opportunities for improvement and build a more resilient foundation for sustainable growth.

Survival should never become the permanent business strategy.

UK businesses need the financial confidence to move beyond short-term survival and start planning for their future again.

Break the cycle. Build financial resilience.

entries.title: MTD for Income Tax: qualifying income, not profit
entries.summary: An illustrative sole-trader example showing how gross qualifying income differs from profit and when MTD Income Tax applies.

posts.text:
MTD for Income Tax: your turnover may matter more than your profit.

Consider an illustrative café owner: £42,000 in annual sales, £30,000 in expenses and £12,000 profit.

HMRC uses qualifying income — broadly, gross income from self-employment and property before expenses — to decide when Making Tax Digital for Income Tax applies. In this example, the relevant amount is £42,000, not £12,000.

For a sole trader with no exemption, qualifying income over £30,000 in 2025/26 means MTD starts on 6 April 2027. The next phase, from 6 April 2028, applies where 2026/27 qualifying income exceeds £20,000.

PAYE wages, dividends, pensions and partnership profit shares are excluded from this qualifying-income calculation. LTD company turnover is not included either.

Before making plans, check your Self Assessment figures, possible exemptions and compatible software. Getting the threshold right is the first step.

More from AU's Knowledge Centre:
https://www.accounting-universe.co.uk/knowledge-centre.html?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=mtd_income_20261123

At AU Finance & Advisory, we understand the financial challenges facing UK travel and hospitality businesses.

Smart technology improves the journey. Human expertise improves the experience. Financial control protects the business.

entries.title: Late payment: statutory interest and compensation
entries.summary: An illustrative calculation of interest and compensation on qualifying overdue commercial invoices.

posts.text:
LATE PAYMENT DOESN'T HAVE TO MEAN LOST MONEY

Did you know that UK businesses may be entitled to claim statutory interest and fixed compensation when commercial invoices are paid late?

Under the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998, qualifying B2B debts can attract statutory interest at 8% above the applicable Bank of England reference rate.

Let's look at a practical example.

A £5,000 invoice became overdue in October 2026 and remained unpaid for 45 days.

Assuming statutory interest applies:

Statutory interest rate: 11.75% per annum

8% + 3.75% (Bank of England reference rate at 30 June 2026)

Interest calculation:
£5,000 × 11.75% × 45 ÷ 365 = £72.43

Fixed compensation: £70

Total additional amount potentially recoverable: £142.43

The statutory fixed compensation depends on the amount owed:
• Under £1,000 — £40
• £1,000 to £9,999.99 — £70
• £10,000 or more — £100

These amounts are in addition to statutory interest where the legislation applies.

Why does this matter?

Late payments can seriously affect working capital, even in otherwise profitable businesses.

Effective credit control, regular debtor reviews and realistic cash flow forecasting help businesses protect liquidity and reduce unnecessary financial pressure.

At AU Finance & Advisory, we help UK businesses strengthen financial control, improve cash flow visibility and make better-informed financial decisions.

Are late-paying customers affecting your business?

Note: Statutory entitlements depend on the circumstances and contractual terms. The example is illustrative.

posts.text:
Paying staff early for Christmas? Check the date on your payroll submission.

For UK pubs, restaurants and other businesses, December wages may be paid earlier than the normal payday.

HMRC's October 2026 Employer Bulletin confirms a crucial detail: when you pay employees early over Christmas, your Full Payment Submission (FPS) should still show their usual or contractual payday.

For example:
• Actual payment: Friday 18 December 2026
• Normal contractual payday: Thursday 31 December 2026
• Date to enter on the FPS: 31 December 2026

Submit the FPS on or before the usual payday.

Why does this matter? Reporting an earlier date can affect employees receiving Universal Credit.

Before December payroll, check:
• The usual payday in employees' contracts
• The payment date entered in your payroll software
• The deadline for submitting the FPS

entries.title: Business growth and working capital
entries.summary: Why higher sales targets need realistic cash flow forecasts, funding assumptions and downside scenarios.

posts.text:
A new iwoca survey of SME finance professionals suggests growing ambition among UK small businesses.

37% report clients raising revenue targets; 34% report higher hiring ambitions.

But growth needs working capital. Higher sales don't automatically mean more cash.

#UKBusiness

UK small businesses are planning for growth again. But can their cash flow keep up?

A new survey of SME finance professionals by UK business lender iwoca, published today, suggests that some British small businesses are becoming more ambitious about growth.

According to the iwoca SME Expert Index:

• 37% of finance professionals surveyed report that their SME clients have increased revenue targets.
• 34% report that their clients have raised their hiring ambitions.

These findings reflect the experiences of the professionals surveyed, rather than the UK small business sector as a whole. Nevertheless, they offer an encouraging indication of business confidence.

But growing a business isn't simply about generating more sales.

New customers may mean additional staff, more stock, higher operating costs and more money tied up in unpaid invoices.

A business can be profitable and growing, yet still struggle to pay its bills.

Before committing to expansion, business owners need to consider:

• How much additional working capital will growth require?
• Will customer payments arrive in time to cover rising costs?
• How will increased spending affect profitability?
• What happens if sales grow more slowly than expected?

Growth should create opportunities, not financial pressure.

Successful expansion requires more than ambitious sales targets. It requires realistic cash flow forecasts and a clear understanding of the financial risks.

Source: iwoca SME Expert Index, 17 November 2026.

#UKBusiness #SmallBusinessUK #BusinessGrowth #CashFlow #FinancialPlanning

entries.title: Your customer pays late. Your bills do not wait.
entries.summary: How overdue customer invoices can put pressure on supplier payments, payroll and business cash flow.

posts.text:
Your customer pays late. Your bills don't wait.

New UK research: 28% of businesses affected by late payments struggled to pay their own bills.

An overdue invoice isn't just an accounting problem. It can put an otherwise profitable business at risk.

#SmallBusinessUK #CashFlow

Your customer pays late. Your bills don't wait.

You've delivered the work. Sent the invoice. Met your side of the agreement.

But the payment hasn't arrived.

Meanwhile, your staff need paying, suppliers expect their money, and HMRC deadlines aren't moving.

New research highlighted by the UK Small Business Commissioner this week reveals that 28% of businesses affected by late payments struggled to pay their own bills as a result.

That's the real cost of late payment. It's not just an overdue invoice. It's the pressure it puts on an otherwise healthy business.

Three things every business owner should keep an eye on:

• How much money is tied up in overdue invoices?
• How long do customers actually take to pay?
• Would your cash flow survive another 30 days without that money?

A profitable business can still run into serious trouble when cash doesn't arrive on time.

Late payments aren't just an administrative nuisance. They're a business risk.

#SmallBusinessUK #CashFlow #LatePayments #FinancialManagement

entries.title: AI is changing accounting. But who checks the AI?
entries.summary: Why professional judgement and verification still matter when accounting work uses AI.

posts.text:
AI can save accountants hours of work. But I've seen it give convincing answers that turned out to be wrong.

In accounting, that can mean VAT errors or costly decisions.

AI is useful. Blind trust isn't.

Who checks the AI?

#UKAccounting #AI

AI is changing accounting. But who checks the AI?

AI can save an enormous amount of time. It can analyse information, process documents, suggest accounting treatments and help with research.

But there's a problem I've encountered myself: AI can give an answer that sounds completely convincing and still be wrong.

In accounting, that matters.

An incorrect VAT treatment, a misclassified transaction or an inaccurate interpretation of HMRC guidance can have consequences well beyond a simple correction in the accounts.

The difficulty isn't always spotting an obvious mistake. It's recognising when something that looks perfectly reasonable needs to be challenged.

I see AI as a valuable tool, but not a substitute for professional judgement, experience and verification.

And I think there's an important question for our profession:

As more accounting work becomes automated, who should ultimately be responsible for checking the result — the software provider, the accountant or the business owner?

I'd be interested to hear how other accountants are approaching this.

#UKAccounting #ArtificialIntelligence #AccountingTechnology

entries.title: Could your VAT accounting method be affecting cash flow?
entries.summary: The timing benefits and trade-offs of VAT cash accounting for eligible businesses.

posts.text:
Could your VAT accounting method be putting unnecessary pressure on cash flow?

Under standard VAT accounting, a business may have to pay VAT on a sales invoice before its customer has paid. HMRC's Cash Accounting Scheme can change that timing for eligible businesses.

Consider an illustrative example: a small consultancy invoices £12,000 including £2,000 VAT, with payment due in 60 days. Under cash accounting, the output VAT would generally be accounted for when payment is received rather than when the invoice is issued.

But there is a trade-off: input VAT on supplier purchases is generally reclaimed only after those suppliers have been paid.

The scheme is not automatically advantageous for every business. Restaurants with mostly immediate card takings, businesses with significant unpaid purchases, and those using other VAT schemes may see little benefit or face different rules.

Before changing methods, compare actual payment patterns, supplier terms and VAT liabilities over several periods.

When did you last review whether your VAT accounting method still suits your business?

VAT due before your customer pays? HMRC’s Cash Accounting Scheme may help eligible businesses align VAT payments with receipts. But input VAT recovery is delayed too. Check both sides of the cash flow before switching. #UKBusiness #VAT

entries.title: When the accounts reveal a worrying trend
entries.summary: A discussion of routine accounting, warning signs and the scope of financial advice.

posts.text:
Your accountant files everything on time. But your margins are shrinking and nobody mentions it.

Has your accountant done their job? Or should financial advice be a separate, paid service?

Business owners and accountants: where do you draw the line?

#UKAccounting

Your accountant keeps your VAT returns, payroll and annual accounts up to date. But what happens when the figures start telling a worrying story?

Take a restaurant that’s busy most evenings but finding it increasingly difficult to cover its bills. Staff costs have risen, supplier prices are higher, and the bank balance isn’t reflecting all those bookings.

The accounts may be perfectly accurate. The problem is that nobody has discussed what those figures mean for the business.

Of course, preparing accounts and providing ongoing financial advice are different services, with different responsibilities and fees.

But here’s something worth discussing.

If an accountant notices a worrying trend while doing the routine work, should they bring it to the client’s attention, even when advisory services aren’t included in the engagement?

Personally, I think there’s a difference between providing detailed financial advice and simply pointing out something that deserves attention.

I’d be interested to hear what business owners and fellow accountants think. Where would you draw the line?

#UKAccounting #BusinessAdvisory #HospitalityFinance

posts.text:

https://www.accounting-universe.co.uk/mtd-income-tax-missed-november-2026-deadline.html

Missed the 7 November MTD quarterly deadline? Here's what matters next.

If you're a sole trader within Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, your second quarterly update was due on 7 November 2026.

HMRC will not issue penalty points for late quarterly updates during the 2026/27 tax year. But that does not mean the reporting obligation has disappeared.

Consider a self-employed café operator recording sales through a till system, expenses in accounting software and supplier payments through a separate bank account.

Before submitting the update, check that records are complete, transactions are correctly categorised and income has not been duplicated. HMRC does not require final tax adjustments at the quarterly stage.

1. What must be paid in the next 14 days?
2. Which sales haven't turned into cash?

entries.title: Profitable on paper, short of cash?
entries.summary: How payment timing, supplier deposits and other commitments can separate reported profit from available cash.

posts.text:
Profitable on paper. Short of cash in the bank?

For hospitality and travel businesses, VAT, supplier deposits and delayed customer payments can create a cash squeeze.

A rolling 13-week cash flow forecast helps spot the gap before payments fall due.

#CashFlow

Your business is profitable. So why is there no cash in the bank?

Profit and cash are not the same thing.

A hospitality or travel business can report a healthy profit while struggling to cover supplier invoices, VAT or payroll.

The reasons may include:
- Customers paying later than expected.
- Deposits paid to suppliers months before the final sale.
- VAT liabilities building up while cash is being spent elsewhere.
- Loan repayments and equipment purchases reducing available funds.

A monthly profit and loss report alone won't reveal the full picture.

The practical step? Review a rolling 13-week cash flow forecast alongside your management accounts.

At AU Finance & Advisory, we help businesses understand not just whether they're profitable, but whether they have the cash to keep moving forward.

#CashFlowManagement #HospitalityFinance #ManagementAccounting

entries.title: Who challenges the numbers?
entries.summary: Turning accurate accounting records into useful questions about margins, contribution and cash flow.

posts.text:
Your accountant prepares the numbers. But who challenges them?

A set of accurate accounts can tell you what happened last year.

It may not tell you why profitability has deteriorated, which customers are becoming less valuable, or whether your business can afford its next major commitment.

For many growing UK businesses, the gap is not a lack of accounting information. It is a lack of financial interpretation.

Management should be able to answer:

• Which activities generate the strongest contribution?
• Where are costs increasing faster than revenue?
• How reliable are our next 13 weeks of cash flow?
• What happens to profitability if our assumptions prove wrong?
• Which decisions require immediate attention?

Financial reporting becomes valuable when it supports decisions — not simply when the numbers reconcile.

Good accounting establishes the facts. Good financial management helps determine what to do next.

#ManagementAccounting #FinancialManagement #UKBusiness

Your accountant prepares the numbers. But who challenges them?

Accurate accounts show what happened. Financial analysis explains why — and what to do next.

Good accounting establishes facts. Good financial management drives better decisions.

#ManagementAccounting #UKBusiness

entries.title: Opening a second restaurant: test the financial case
entries.summary: Why an expansion model should include working capital, opening delays and lower-than-forecast sales.

posts.text:
Opening a second restaurant? Revenue growth alone doesn't prove value creation.

Model fit-out costs, working capital, delays and a 15% sales shortfall.

Can the existing business fund the downside without putting its own cash at risk?

#UKHospitality

Opening a second restaurant? Growth in revenue does not always mean growth in value.

A successful first location can make expansion look like the obvious next step. But the financial case deserves more scrutiny than a sales forecast.

Consider an illustrative scenario: a new site is expected to generate £750,000 in annual revenue. Before signing a lease, management needs to understand more than its projected operating profit.

What happens if sales are 15% below forecast for the first six months?

How much working capital will be tied up before the site reaches stable trading?

Will the existing business have to fund early losses, recruitment and supplier commitments?

And what is the financial impact if opening takes three months longer than planned?

A robust investment model should connect site-level contribution, capital expenditure, cash flow, funding requirements and downside scenarios.

The objective is not simply to demonstrate that expansion could work. It is to establish whether the business can withstand the risks.

What would be your most important financial test before opening another location?

#UKHospitality #FinancialModelling #BusinessExpansion

entries.title: Restaurant break-even: how many covers do you need?
entries.summary: A worked illustration of contribution per cover and the number of covers needed to meet daily fixed costs.

posts.text:
How many covers does your restaurant need to break even on a quiet Tuesday?

A full dining room isn't the only measure of financial health. Knowing your break-even point helps you make better decisions about staffing, opening hours and menu pricing.

Here's a simple illustration (figures are hypothetical):

• Average revenue per cover, excluding VAT: £30
• Variable costs per cover: £15
• Contribution per cover: £15
• Daily fixed costs: £900

Break-even covers = £900 ÷ £15 = 60.

Below 60 covers, the day doesn't cover those fixed costs. Above 60, each additional cover contributes towards profit, assuming the costs and sales mix stay similar.

Your real number depends on food and drink margins, labour patterns, rent, utilities and other costs — and it can change by day of the week.

November is the time to stress-test your December trading plan.

For pubs, restaurants and event venues, a full bookings diary can look reassuring. But it does not tell you whether the month will actually generate healthy profit and cash flow.

Five checks worth making before the festive rush:

1. Bookings vs earned revenue — distinguish confirmed reservations, deposits received and services delivered.
2. Menu gross profit — review margins after promotions, waste and supplier cost changes.
3. Labour planning — forecast staffing costs by shift and expected demand, not only last month's percentage.
4. Payment timing — map supplier due dates and payroll against expected receipts.
5. Downside scenarios — what happens if sales are 10% below plan or labour costs rise by 5%?

A one-page weekly dashboard can help spot issues while there is still time to act.

entries.title: Business rates and your 2027/28 forecast
entries.summary: A dated overview of Budget announcements affecting qualifying hospitality properties in England.

posts.text:
Own a pub or restaurant in England?

From April 2027, business rates (tax on commercial premises) are changing:
• Eligible pubs: 35% relief, up from 15%.
• Qualifying small hospitality properties: 100% relief up to £18k rateable value.

Check your 2027/28 cash flow.

England's hospitality businesses: is your 2027/28 business rates forecast ready?

The UK Government's Autumn Budget 2026 (28 October) announced changes for qualifying properties in England from 1 April 2027:

• Business rates relief for eligible pubs, social clubs and most live music venues is set to rise from 15% to 35% in 2027/28 and 2028/29. Live music venues with a rateable value of £1 million or more will remain at 15%.
• For businesses eligible for Small Business Rates Relief, the full-relief rateable value threshold for qualifying retail, hospitality and leisure properties will increase from £12,000 to £18,000, with tapered relief up to £21,000.
• Annual business rates bill increases for qualifying retail, hospitality and leisure properties will be capped by CPI inflation in 2027/28 and 2028/29. Exceptions include improvements that increase a property's rateable value and the loss of certain other reliefs.

These measures have been announced, but detailed regulations and guidance are still to follow. Eligibility depends on the business and property circumstances; the 35% relief does not apply to ordinary restaurants or cafés simply because they are in hospitality.

For independent pubs, cafés and restaurants, now is the time to review rateable values, property costs and cash-flow forecasts — rather than assume headline relief will automatically apply.

At AU Finance & Advisory, we help UK hospitality businesses assess financial changes and plan with confidence.

entries.title: What would a hospitality VAT reduction mean?
entries.summary: A hypothetical example comparing lower customer prices with a higher business margin.

posts.text:
If hospitality VAT were cut from 20% to 10%, who should benefit — the customer, the business, or both?

UKHospitality is calling for a 10% rate. A simple example shows the choice facing restaurant owners.

Today, a £120 bill consists of £100 revenue and £20 VAT.

If the proposed reduction were introduced:

• Passing it on in full would bring the bill down to £110. The customer saves £10; the restaurant’s revenue remains £100.

• Keeping the bill at £120 would leave £109.09 in revenue and £10.91 in VAT. The restaurant gains £9.09 before costs.

An operator could also share the benefit: reduce menu prices partly and retain the rest to support margins, staffing or investment.

As a restaurant owner or customer, which approach would you favour — and why?

#Hospitality #VAT

If hospitality VAT fell from 20% to 10%, a £120 restaurant bill could:

• Fall to £110, keeping revenue unchanged.
• Stay at £120, giving the business £9.09 extra revenue before costs.

Lower prices, stronger margins — or a mix of both?

What would you choose?
